content: Non-allergic rhinitis is characterized by dysfunction and non-infectious inflammation of the nasal mucosa, triggered by factors other than allergens or microbes. It is a common condition, affecting approximately 10% to 20% of the population. Patients with non-allergic rhinitis typically experience symptoms such as nasal obstruction, anterior rhinorrhea or post-nasal drip, and sneezing. Various subtypes of non-allergic rhinitis exist, depending on the specific triggers, which may include occupational exposures, cigarette smoke, hormonal changes, medications, certain foods, or age-related factors. On a cellular and molecular level, different mechanisms underlie the disease, but these are not yet fully understood. Consequently, many patients with non-allergic rhinitis lack effective treatment options due to the limited understanding and recognition of the underlying pathophysiology. Intranasal corticosteroids are frequently prescribed for patients with rhinitis or rhinosinusitis symptoms, including those with non-allergic rhinitis. However, the efficacy of intranasal corticosteroids in managing non-allergic rhinitis remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of intranasal corticosteroids in the treatment of non-allergic rhinitis. The Cochrane ENT Information Specialist conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, for both published and unpublished trials. The search was completed on July 1, 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intranasal corticosteroids (administered in any form or dosage) with placebo, no intervention, or other active treatments in adults and children aged 12 years or older were included. The review included 34 studies involving 4,452 participants, but only 13 studies provided data for the primary comparison of intranasal corticosteroids versus placebo. Most participants were identified as having perennial rhinitis symptoms with negative allergy tests. Specific subtypes of non-allergic rhinitis, such as pregnancy rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, or senile rhinitis, were only included in a few studies. The majority of studies were conducted in secondary or tertiary healthcare settings, and none reported outcomes beyond three months of follow-up. The dosage of intranasal corticosteroids ranged from 50 µg to 2,000 µg daily. When comparing intranasal corticosteroids to placebo, 13 studies (2,045 participants) provided data. These studies used various scoring systems to assess patient-reported disease severity, and the data were pooled using standardized mean differences (SMD). Intranasal corticosteroids may improve patient-reported disease severity, as measured by the total nasal symptom score, compared to placebo at up to four weeks (SMD -0.74, 95% CI -1.15 to -0.33; 4 studies; 131 participants; I² = 22%), but the certainty of this evidence is low. Between four weeks and three months, the evidence becomes very uncertain (SMD -0.24, 95% CI -0.67 to 0.20; 3 studies; 85 participants; I² = 0%), with very low certainty. Intranasal corticosteroids may slightly improve patient-reported disease severity, as measured by changes in the total nasal symptom score from baseline, compared to placebo at up to four weeks (SMD -0.15, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.05; 4 studies; 1,465 participants; I² = 35%), but this evidence is also of low certainty. Four studies assessed the risk of epistaxis and found that intranasal corticosteroids probably increase the risk of this adverse effect (65 per 1,000 in the corticosteroid group versus 31 per 1,000 in the placebo group; risk ratio [RR] 2.10, 95% CI 1.24 to 3.57; 4 studies; 1,174 participants; I² = 0%), with moderate-certainty evidence. The absolute risk difference was 0.04, and the number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) was 25 (95% CI 16.7 to 100). Only one study reported numerical data on quality of life, showing a higher score in the intranasal corticosteroid group (152.3 versus 145.6; SF-12v2 range 0 to 800), but this difference disappeared at longer-term follow-up (148.4 versus 145.6). The certainty of this evidence was low. Two studies provided data on objective airflow measurements, but the results could not be pooled due to differences in measurement methods. Neither study found significant differences between the corticosteroid and placebo groups (rhinomanometry SMD -0.46, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.14; 44 participants; peak expiratory flow rate SMD 0.78, 95% CI -0.47 to 2.03; 11 participants), with very low-certainty evidence. Intranasal corticosteroids likely result in little or no difference in the risk of other adverse events compared to placebo (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.12; 3 studies; 1,130 participants; I² = 0%), with moderate-certainty evidence. When comparing intranasal corticosteroids to other treatments, only one or a few studies assessed each comparison (e.g., corticosteroids versus saline irrigation, intranasal antihistamines, capsaicin, cromoglycate sodium, ipratropium bromide, or combinations of these treatments). Due to the limited number of studies, it is uncertain whether there are differences between intranasal corticosteroids and other active treatments for any of the reported outcomes. In conclusion, the certainty of the evidence for most outcomes in this review was low or very low. It remains unclear whether intranasal corticosteroids reduce patient-reported disease severity in non-allergic rhinitis patients compared to placebo when measured at up to three months. However, intranasal corticosteroids likely increase the risk of epistaxis. The lack of studies comparing intranasal corticosteroids to other treatment modalities makes it challenging to draw definitive conclusions.
